proposals.name: Cartoon dependence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption would make little sense or lose its force if the exact cartoon changed; score 0 when it could accompany many unrelated cartoons.
proposals.rationale: R10, R35, and R40 use broadly reusable real-estate or housing language, whereas R41 and R60 depend closely on the elephant-elevator and long-distance telephone setups.

proposals.name: Causal grounding
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption supplies a plausible motive, explanation, or reason for the depicted absurdity; score 0 when it merely reacts to the image without explaining anything about it.
proposals.rationale: R01 explains why the bear shops for fish, and R12 gives the magician-flight-attendant a concrete rationale; R22 and R28 offer little explanation for the kitchen or moon scenes.

proposals.name: Multi-detail integration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the joke connects two or more conspicuous cartoon details in one coherent idea; score 0 when it uses only a generic reference to the overall oddity.
proposals.rationale: R03 integrates the miniature person, human resources, and firing; R41 combines the elephant with the elevator idiom. R30 and R57 mainly attach a simple phrase to one visible feature.

proposals.name: Speaker-role fidelity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the line sounds natural for a particular depicted speaker given that character’s role and situation; score 0 when no plausible depicted speaker could say it.
proposals.rationale: R17 and R49 make the miniature-person device part of an office power exchange, while R13 and R30 provide lines with weakly defined speakers and situations.

proposals.name: Interpersonal specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption establishes a clear relationship, status difference, or conflict between depicted characters; score 0 when it contains no meaningful interpersonal dynamic.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R17 turn the office scene into a specific superior-subordinate interaction; R10 and R35 focus on generic property language without developing the buyers’ relationship.

proposals.name: Coherent reframing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption shifts the cartoon into an unexpected domain while preserving a clear structural mapping to the visible scene; score 0 when the new domain is merely associative or random.
proposals.rationale: R04 reframes the faced moon through the poop-emoji comparison, and R59 maps the alien arrival onto a political firearm reference; R28 and R53 introduce topical associations with little structural mapping.

proposals.name: Concrete consequence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption imagines an immediate, specific practical consequence of the bizarre situation; score 0 when it offers only an abstract observation or label.
proposals.rationale: R05 predicts downstairs neighbors’ reaction, R09 anticipates needing a safety net, and R58 identifies the cost of removing a lawyer. R30 and R42 lack comparable situational consequences.

proposals.name: Idiomatic collision
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a familiar idiom is deliberately twisted so that the cartoon’s literal detail creates a second precise meaning; score 0 when the phrase remains literal, clichéd, or unrelated to the image.
proposals.rationale: R41 transforms elephant in the room through the elevator setting, and R60 turns please hold into an exact telephone-and-IRS collision. R19 and R30 use familiar word associations without comparable idiomatic transformation.

proposals.name: Exact wordplay
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a pun exploits an exact object, sound, or name and both meanings are immediately clear; score 0 when the wordplay is tenuous, generic, or only nominally connected to the cartoon.
proposals.rationale: R50 makes bark and cotton bale serve the sheep-dog confusion, while R51 builds repeatedly on ewe. R19’s spare ribs and R30’s phase rely on simpler surface puns.

proposals.name: Narrative continuation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption advances a miniature story by implying a prior event, current action, or likely next development; score 0 when it simply restates what is visibly present.
proposals.rationale: R02 supplies the bear’s previous fishing ordeal, R31 explains the wish that produced the island encounter, and R47 imagines the wife’s subsequent reaction.

proposals.name: Punchline economy
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording is compact, with a clear setup and a final phrase that delivers the reversal; score 0 when it meanders, buries the turn, or has no distinct punchline.
proposals.rationale: R12, R41, and R60 reach their reversals quickly through compact conversational lines, while R10 and R35 use longer but comparatively diffuse real-estate observations.

proposals.name: Reference integration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a cultural, political, or current-events reference is essential to interpreting the cartoon and illuminates its specific premise; score 0 when it is detachable name-dropping.
proposals.rationale: R36 integrates social distancing with the baseball players’ protective gear, and R43 connects kitchen supplies with toilet-paper scarcity. R28 and R53 mention recognizable topics without making them necessary to the visual joke.

proposals.name: Visible-detail fidelity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption accurately preserves the depicted characters, objects, and relationships while adding compatible fictional implications; score 0 when it ignores, overwrites, or contradicts the salient visual details.
proposals.rationale: R43 retains the kitchen’s shopping context and the robot as an interlocutor, while R18 preserves the delivery and payment relationship. R22 and R53 introduce premises largely detached from the pictured kitchen interaction.

proposals.name: Immediate accessibility
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a reader can understand the joke from the cartoon description and caption without obscure decoding or missing context; score 0 when the intended connection remains opaque.
proposals.rationale: R02 and R24 communicate their premises directly through familiar situations, whereas R32 and R46 require less obvious interpretation of the sandcastle and butterfly transformations.

proposals.name: Playful tonal fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption adopts a clear, proportionate comic attitude toward the cartoon’s absurdity and produces a playful payoff; score 0 when it is flat, needlessly grim, or hostile without comic development.
proposals.rationale: R05 and R47 use light domestic consequences to heighten the absurd scenes, while R08 and R14 lean on distress or hardship without developing an equally strong playful payoff.

proposals.name: Live-news timestamping
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption contains references whose meaning or salience depends on a particular news cycle or contemporary moment; judge only visible text, not whether the caption is good.
proposals.rationale: Time-sensitive references such as six-feet distancing in R15, N95 masks in R34, stimulus payments in R46, and Trump in R52 can leave a temporal fingerprint unrelated to cartoon-specific caption quality.

proposals.name: Era-dated cultural idiom
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption uses generationally or historically marked idioms, cultural references, brands, or institutional terms; judge only visible text, not whether the caption is good.
proposals.rationale: References such as “Stairway to Heaven” in R01, “town car” in R13, and mescal in R45 may identify an era or readership convention without measuring fit to the depicted cartoon.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the contest's historical era

proposals.name: Consensus-angle phrasing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption uses the most immediately suggested pun, idiom, or literal reinterpretation of a conspicuous visual element, with little individualized framing; judge only visible text, not whether the caption is good.
proposals.rationale: “Second home” in R05, “downsizing” in R14, “ewe” repetition in R50, and “keeper” in R60 resemble readily available first-thought angles. Their commonness can reflect crowd position rather than cartoon-specific quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream for the cartoon

proposals.name: Practitioner compression
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption is an unusually economical one-liner or fragment with immediate delivery and no explanatory scaffolding; judge only visible text, not whether the caption is good.
proposals.rationale: The terse lines in R01, R05, and R26 show disciplined brevity and confident caption form. Such traces may reflect a serial entrant's practice, which can coexist with but is not identical to cartoon-specific quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the caption format

proposals.name: Deadpan print register
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption uses restrained, plain, low-arousal, print-ready conversational diction and punctuation; judge only visible text, not whether the caption is good.
proposals.rationale: The understated phrasing in R20, R36, and R55 fits a restrained publication register. House-style conformity can influence textual reception while remaining distinct from the caption's actual fit to its cartoon.

proposals.name: Transcription artifacts
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption exhibits catalog or transcription conventions such as lowercase starts, omitted terminal punctuation, ellipses, doubled hyphens, or spacing quirks; judge only visible text, not whether the caption is good.
proposals.rationale: Lowercase presentation in R03, ellipses in R04, and doubled hyphens in R29 and R39 may come from compilation conventions rather than the entrant's wording or cartoon-specific quality.

proposals.name: Familiar social-role framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption frames the joke through a familiar relationship or social role such as spouse, parent, boss, neighbor, or customer; judge only visible text, not whether the caption is good.
proposals.rationale: Domestic and role-based framing appears in R08's wife reference, R11's parent-child exchange, R22's downstairs neighbors, and R57's named payer. These cues can appeal to audience familiarity without being evidence of cartoon-specific quality.

proposals.name: Generic caption-template polish
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption is self-contained, grammatically complete, immediately legible, and shaped like a familiar setup-punchline template with an explicit scene-to-joke mapping; judge only visible text, not whether the caption is good.
proposals.rationale: The polished templates in R10, R30, R44, and R53 are easy to recognize as conventional captions. Generic recognizability can be a nuisance prior even when it does not reflect what this particular cartoon calls for.

proposals.name: Explanatory narrative load
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption contains multiple clauses, named roles, backstory, or explicit explanation of why the situation matters; judge only visible text, not whether the caption is good.
proposals.rationale: R12, R19, R43, and R59 include substantial narrative or explanatory detail. Length and elaboration can systematically affect text-based impressions without measuring the caption's cartoon-specific quality.

proposals.name: Institutional jargon density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption uses legal, bureaucratic, political, or organizational vocabulary and labels; judge only visible text, not whether the caption is good.
proposals.rationale: Legal and institutional wording appears in R10's lawyer reference, R19's human-resources framing, R33's litigation, and R58's political wording. Domain familiarity may create a textual prior independent of how well the line fits its cartoon.

proposals.name: Distinctive-detail anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the joke depends on a specific, distinctive visual detail; score 0 when it could fit many unrelated cartoons.
proposals.rationale: R03 uses the worker's position at the beam's end, while R22 uses the dogs' resemblance to sheep and the cotton-bale confusion.

proposals.name: In-world causal explanation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption invents a coherent reason for the impossible scene; score 0 when it merely labels the absurdity or adds an unrelated premise.
proposals.rationale: R04 explains the miniature person through HR retaliation, and R28 turns the car hoist into a household dining surface.

proposals.name: Layered semantic convergence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when two or more meanings converge cleanly on the pictured situation; score 0 when the line has only one thin, literal reading.
proposals.rationale: R18 combines extinction with the persistence of hats, while R59 connects the moon's face to an emoji and a broader cultural comparison.

proposals.name: Speaker-knowledge authenticity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the speaker's wording reflects what that character would plausibly know, notice, or care about; score 0 when the voice is unmotivated by the depicted speaker.
proposals.rationale: R15 sounds like a bear rationalizing its shopping choice from fishing experience, while R09 sounds like a party guest considering the practical need for a net.

proposals.name: Expectation reversal
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption sharply reverses the audience's expected interpretation while remaining understandable; score 0 when it gives only the obvious reaction to the image.
proposals.rationale: R02 reverses the deserted-island fantasy into a complaint about an underspecified wish, and R25 transforms the usual elephant-in-the-room phrase into elevator etiquette.

proposals.name: Topical-reference integration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a cultural or current reference is tightly fused to the cartoon's visual premise; score 0 when the reference could be pasted onto almost any scene.
proposals.rationale: R37 links baseball equipment and social distancing, while R48 makes the robot's grocery errand part of pandemic-era scarcity behavior.

proposals.name: Implied aftermath
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the line suggests a vivid consequence, prior event, or next event beyond what is shown; score 0 when it stops at naming the visible oddity.
proposals.rationale: R09 anticipates the need to catch the airborne guest, and R39 projects the future cost of removing the lawyer from the engine compartment.

proposals.name: Conversational punch timing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording has a natural setup and lands its strongest turn at the end; score 0 when it is awkwardly phrased, overexplained, or lacks a punch.
proposals.rationale: R10 delays the reveal of who is firing the employee, while R21 ends on the concrete surprise of being charged for beer already in the refrigerator.

proposals.name: Power-relationship inversion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the impossible image creates a sharp, intelligible reversal of authority or status; score 0 when no relationship or power dynamic is used.
proposals.rationale: R04 makes a miniature HR surrogate deliver a firing, and R34 converts the miniature self into a new superior who receives direct reports.

proposals.name: Metaphorical scene extension
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption extends the cartoon's physical impossibility into a coherent metaphor; score 0 when it merely substitutes a generic metaphor unrelated to the depicted action.
proposals.rationale: R24 turns a view of outer space into neighborhood expansion, while R54 makes sinking into a puddle a workplace-overload metaphor.

proposals.name: Object-locked wordplay
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a pun depends precisely on an object, action, or setting shown in the cartoon; score 0 when it is a detachable homonym or word joke.
proposals.rationale: R05 makes 'phase' depend on the moon, and R29 makes 'spare ribs' depend on both the tunnel's apparent anatomy and the chefs' menu.

proposals.name: Mundane-detail realism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an ordinary concrete detail makes the absurd situation feel socially or practically real; score 0 when the caption contains only a broad exclamation.
proposals.rationale: R21 adds a specific household billing grievance to the indoor baseball, while R33 imagines downstairs neighbors reacting to the bowling-room noise.

proposals.name: Self-contained accessibility
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the joke is immediately understandable from the cartoon and caption alone; score 0 when comprehension depends on obscure knowledge or an unexplained reference.
proposals.rationale: R42 relies on the familiar magician's chicken-or-rabbit choice, whereas R53 invokes Elon Musk without clearly connecting his identity to the moon scene.

proposals.name: Non-template angle
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the association is surprising and individualized rather than a stock response; score 0 when it uses the first cliché suggested by the image.
proposals.rationale: R17 uses a sinking-Venice association for the chandelier catch, while R38 gives a more elaborated inventory of rejected lighting fixtures.

proposals.name: Premise continuity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption accepts the cartoon's strange premise and logically continues its situation; score 0 when it abandons the premise for a non sequitur.
proposals.rationale: R35 continues the dinosaur band's rehearsal despite the meteor, while R55 uses the band's music and impending extinction to extend the scene into a fitting song reference.

proposals.name: Dated topical residue
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption contains references to events, policies, public figures, products, or practices that anchor it to a particular news moment; do not judge whether the reference is good.
proposals.rationale: Submission timing can leave date-specific traces without measuring cartoon fit. Examples include the stimulus payment in R10, six-feet-apart language in R41, N95 masks in R46, and live sports in R48.

proposals.name: Consensus visual pun
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption uses the most immediate pun, idiom, or stock association suggested by the visible objects; do not judge whether the resulting joke is good.
proposals.rationale: An obvious first-thought reading can reveal that an entry occupies the consensus end of the submission stream, independently of its intrinsic fit. Examples are “new phase” in R04, “Stairway to Heaven” in R14, and “spare ribs” in R26.

proposals.name: Self-contained polish
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption is a fluent, grammatical, self-contained one-liner with a clearly resolved setup and punch; do not judge whether it is funny or high quality.
proposals.rationale: Smooth completion and familiar caption form are generic-prior signals that a general writer or language model could recognize without contest-specific knowledge. This form appears in R01, R33, and R54, but formal completeness does not establish the best cartoon-specific angle.

proposals.name: Practiced caption compression
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the line is compressed caption-native dialogue that assumes the drawing, omits explanation, and delivers one economical beat; do not judge whether the compression is effective.
proposals.rationale: A serial entrant's familiarity with the format can leave disciplined brevity and refusal to narrate the image, while that same practice may also improve genuine writing skill. Compact examples include R03, R07, and R17.

proposals.name: Compiler typography residue
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the text shows transcription or formatting conventions such as lowercase openings, missing terminal punctuation, ellipses, repeated hyphens, or unusual spacing; do not judge whether the typography is good.
proposals.rationale: The compiler's handling of submitted text can create systematic surface traces unrelated to cartoon fit. Lowercase and absent terminal punctuation appear in R01, repeated hyphens in R31, and an ellipsis in R48.

proposals.name: Shared-context allusion load
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which understanding the caption depends on outside cultural, legal, institutional, celebrity, or specialized-domain knowledge; do not judge whether the allusion is apt.
proposals.rationale: Audience composition and an entrant's assumed readership can make outside-reference density predictive while also sometimes informing the actual joke. Examples include “second amendment” in R15, “democratic elevator” in R29, litigation jargon in R52, and the IRS in R58.

proposals.name: Layered joke accumulation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption retains multiple clauses, punch mechanisms, explanatory tags, or alternative associations in one line; do not judge whether the layering improves the joke.
proposals.rationale: Revision, brainstorming, or outside assistance can leave a visible composite line containing several joke beats, and revision can also affect genuine quality. Layering is evident in R12, R18, R50, and R60.

proposals.name: House-style tonal register
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption uses plain, restrained, everyday conversational diction and understated social framing; do not judge whether that register suits the cartoon.
proposals.rationale: A publication's recurring register can imprint captions with dry understatement and ordinary workplace or domestic diction, independently of cartoon-specific merit, while register can also affect contest suitability. Examples include R03, R17, and R42.

proposals.name: Social-risk edge load
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption uses violent, sexual, partisan, insulting, taboo, or otherwise provocative framing; do not judge whether the material is acceptable or effective.
proposals.rationale: Audience reaction and social norms can make provocative wording predictive without making it inherently better for the drawing. Such framing appears in the gun reference in R15, the adolescent-taste reference in R30, mating language in R45, and the lawyer threat in R47.

proposals.name: Domestic-role framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption interprets the scene through family, spousal, household, neighbor, or parent-child roles and obligations; do not judge whether that framing is good.
proposals.rationale: Entrant background and audience demographics can favor familiar domestic frames that correlate with reception but are not themselves evidence of cartoon fit. Examples include the wife in R05, father-and-son framing in R10, downstairs neighbors in R13, and marriage in R44.

proposals.name: Salient-detail integration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption makes two or more prominent depicted particulars work together in one coherent joke; score 0 when it merely states the odd premise or could fit almost any scene.
proposals.rationale: The dense-favored lines connect multiple elements in R16, R20, and R57, whereas simpler one-detail associations appear in R02 and R08.

proposals.name: Literalized idiom
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a recognizable idiom gains a precise second, literal meaning from the pictured situation; score 0 when no idiom is present or the wording remains purely literal.
proposals.rationale: R16 literalizes “elephant in the room,” while R45 turns “downsizing” into the miniature person; R42 provides another metaphor physically enacted by the cartoon.

proposals.name: Causal consequence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption derives a specific practical or social consequence from the impossible scene; score 0 when it only labels, describes, or loosely comments on the scene.
proposals.rationale: R10, R12, and R32 imagine concrete consequences of the depicted situations, unlike more associative lines such as R37 and R49.

proposals.name: Speaker-role fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the apparent speaker’s knowledge, diction, and attitude fit a clearly inferable role in the cartoon; score 0 when the voice could belong to anyone or conflicts with the scene.
proposals.rationale: R14 fits a spouse reacting to a household chore, while R43 fits an HR-related speaker; R03 and R09 illustrate less clearly grounded speaking perspectives.

proposals.name: Relationship dynamics
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption establishes a specific power relationship, conflict, or intimacy between depicted participants; score 0 when it supplies no meaningful interpersonal dynamic.
proposals.rationale: R17 and R28 exploit the boss-subordinate relationship created by the miniature self, while R55 builds a conflict between the wish-maker and the disappointed visitor.

proposals.name: Topical fusion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a cultural or current reference is transformed by the exact visual premise and adds a fresh interpretation; score 0 when the reference is merely name-dropped and would work unchanged elsewhere.
proposals.rationale: R20 fuses pandemic behavior with the baseball scene, and R50 fuses gun-law language with aliens; R33 and R35 show similarly topical but more detachable references.

proposals.name: Double-duty wordplay
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a word or phrase has two precise meanings, both essential to the joke and both anchored in the cartoon; score 0 when the pun is forced, incidental, or unrelated to the image.
proposals.rationale: R27 uses “ewe” to connect sheep and conversation, while R38 exploits “town car”; R44 demonstrates a broader object-based wordplay pattern.

proposals.name: Mundane-absurd contrast
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an ordinary concern is treated as normal or urgent within an impossible setting, creating sharp incongruity; score 0 when the caption uses the same register as the scene or simply restates it.
proposals.rationale: R12 treats beer billing as the concern amid indoor baseball, and R29 treats dinner logistics as normal during a living-room car repair; R41 uses a comparable captivity-related contrast.

proposals.name: Payoff surprise
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the ending sharply redirects the reader toward an unexpected but coherent interpretation; score 0 when the punchline is an obvious first association or lacks a turn.
proposals.rationale: R21, R30, and R60 deliver unexpected reframings of elevators, the moon, and shopping; R02 and R06 rely on more immediately predictable associations.

proposals.name: Off-screen backstory
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption implies a concise unseen situation that plausibly explains the cartoon and expands its comic world; score 0 when it adds no situation or introduces an arbitrary one.
proposals.rationale: R39 implies a hidden lawyer-related predicament inside the engine, and R55 supplies a prior wish that explains the island encounter; R53 similarly invents an unseen institutional interaction.

proposals.name: Cartoon-specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when replacing the cartoon with a different scene would break the caption’s meaning or humor; score 0 when the caption remains equally suitable for many unrelated cartoons.
proposals.rationale: R02, R06, and R08 use broad real-estate concepts that transfer readily, while R16 and R58 depend on distinctive physical arrangements.

proposals.name: Freshness over cliché
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a familiar phrase, reference, or association is materially twisted into a new comic idea; score 0 when it reproduces a stock expression with minimal alteration.
proposals.rationale: R18, R37, R47, and R51 draw on familiar evolution, lunar, botanical, and sinking-related associations, making cliché resistance a useful distinction.

proposals.name: Interpretive clarity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a reader can immediately reconstruct the intended connection from the cartoon and caption without an unexplained semantic leap; score 0 when the connection is ambiguous, obscure, or internally unclear.
proposals.rationale: The connections in R03, R07, R15, and R25 require substantial interpretation, whereas R16 and R32 make their comic mechanisms readily recoverable.

proposals.name: Spoken naturalness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption sounds like a polished, idiomatic utterance a person would naturally say; score 0 when syntax, diction, or cadence feels awkward, malformed, or implausible.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R07 contain awkward or difficult-to-process phrasing, while R41 and R46 demonstrate more immediately conversational delivery.

proposals.name: Secondary-detail leverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the humor depends on supporting props, background details, setting, or secondary characters as well as the central anomaly; score 0 when all such details are ignored.
proposals.rationale: R20 uses the catcher’s mask and distancing behavior, R57 uses the room’s implied neighbors, and R58 uses the sheep’s visual similarity and a cotton bale.

proposals.name: News-cycle topicality
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the caption uses time-bound news, politics, public figures, or live events; do not judge whether this makes the caption good.
proposals.rationale: A live reference can leave a dated textual trace and attract generic topicality effects independent of cartoon-specific craft. Examples include “n95 mask” in R06, “trump” and “crusades” in R16, and “six feet apart” in R47.

proposals.name: Consensus-first visual reading
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the wording presents the most immediate, widely shareable association suggested by the drawing; do not judge whether that association is good.
proposals.rationale: An obvious first-thought line may reflect early or consensus positioning among many submissions rather than distinctive construction. “Spare ribs” in R25, “new phase” in R26, and “chicken or rabbit” in R52 show this fingerprint.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream for the cartoon

proposals.name: Generic caption polish
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the caption has compact, complete, immediately legible setup-punch packaging familiar from generic caption examples; do not judge whether it is funny or apt.
proposals.rationale: Well-formed caption-shaped language is easy for a general-purpose prior to recognize without requiring contest-specific taste. R03, R20, R32, and R56 use concise, self-contained conventional joke formats.

proposals.name: Serial-entrant fluency
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the caption shows practiced-format discipline through economical length, assumed visual context, confident speaker voice, and refusal to explain; do not judge whether the result is good.
proposals.rationale: Repeated practice can produce recognizable rhythm and economy that are separable from cartoon-specific merit. The clipped dialogue in R01 and R03, and the confidently scene-dependent lines in R11 and R20, exhibit this trace.
proposals.upstream_parent: entrant’s serial practice in the format

proposals.name: House-style deadpan register
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the caption uses restrained, clean, conversational, understated deadpan rather than hype, exposition, or overt theatricality; do not judge whether that register is desirable.
proposals.rationale: A venue’s preferred register can shape wording independently of the particular cartoon, while also sometimes overlapping with genuine fit. R05, R11, R24, and R27 use economical understated domestic or conversational framing.

proposals.name: Transcription typography quirks
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the caption displays formatting conventions or artifacts such as lowercase starts, ellipses, repeated punctuation, emoji, dash styles, or unusual terminal-punctuation habits; do not judge whether the formatting improves the caption.
proposals.rationale: Compilation practices can create text-visible regularities unrelated to caption content. Lowercase and ellipsis patterns appear in R01 and R10, while repeated punctuation and emoji-like wording appear in R17 and R33.

proposals.name: Polarizing social salience
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the caption invokes partisan identity, contentious institutions, public-figure affiliation, or culture-war vocabulary; do not judge whether the reference is relevant or good.
proposals.rationale: Socially charged terms can create audience-related textual effects without indicating cartoon-specific quality. Examples include “second amendment” in R04, “trump” in R16, “elon musk” in R42, and “democratic” in R53.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience social salience and reputational effects

proposals.name: Explicit scene explanation
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the caption names, paraphrases, or explains the visible anomaly or tells the reader how to interpret it; do not judge whether the explanation is effective.
proposals.rationale: Explicit visual anchoring is a surface property that may be overvalued by generic text heuristics despite not being inherent quality. R35 spells out the “elephant in the room” premise, while R55 and R58 directly explain the bear or sheep-dog situation.

proposals.name: Pun and idiom density
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the caption relies on homophones, double meanings, transformed idioms, or concentrated wordplay; do not judge whether the wordplay is clever.
proposals.rationale: Wordplay density is an easily detected lexical channel that need not track cartoon-specific success. Examples include “ewe” repetition in R17, fishing “sconces” and “keeper” in R21, “spare ribs” in R25, and “roots” in R46.

proposals.name: Recognizable cultural allusion
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the caption uses a recognizable song, emoji, stock phrase, institutional shorthand, or other evergreen cultural reference not required by the drawing; do not judge whether the allusion is good.
proposals.rationale: Familiar references can trigger broad cultural-recognition priors independently of cartoon-specific construction. “Stairway to heaven” appears in R09, “poop emoji” in R33, “IRS” in R56, and the stock magic choice “chicken or rabbit” in R52.

proposals.name: Misdirection Away From Visual Absurdity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption deliberately ignores the most obvious strange element in the cartoon (e.g., a propeller hat) to deliver a punchline about a completely unrelated, secondary, or darkly implied topic. Score 0 if the caption directly and obviously jokes about the primary visual absurdity.
proposals.rationale: Dense rewards captions that subvert expectations. R14 (eating sophomores instead of a hat joke) and R29 (extinction instead of a hat) are rated highly by dense, whereas the scorecard misses this layer and favors obvious jokes.

proposals.name: Seamless Idiom Recontextualization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if a common idiom or metaphorical phrase is twisted so that its figurative meaning is applied perfectly to the literal absurdity of the cartoon. Score 0 if a metaphor is merely visualized literally without adding a comedic twist.
proposals.rationale: The dense model values clever plays on idioms over straightforward jokes. R43 ('elephant in the room') and R23 ('town car') recontextualize language brilliantly, scoring high on dense but low on scorecard.

proposals.name: Deadpan Underreaction To Surreal Danger
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the speaker treats a highly dangerous, bizarre, or impossible situation as a mundane, bureaucratic, or trivial inconvenience. Score 0 if the speaker reacts with shock or directly addresses the impossibility of the situation.
proposals.rationale: The dense model values a casual tone in the face of absurdity. R02 (setting up the net for a cannon) and R44 (arriving early as if magic equals speed) contrast with the scorecard's preference for straightforward observations.

proposals.name: Absurd Causation Or Hyperbolic Backstory
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption explains the visual weirdness by inventing a wildly exaggerated, historically grand, or completely surreal backstory. Score 0 if the caption provides a mundane, generic explanation for the scene.
proposals.rationale: Dense rewards creative world-building that expands the cartoon's universe. R49 ('crusade') and R53 ('Trump cancelled the crusades') score high on dense but low on scorecard, showing a gap in recognizing hyperbolic excuses.

proposals.name: Bureaucratic Or Cynical Satire
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption injects a dark, political, or highly cynical real-world societal rule into a fantasy/cartoon scenario. Score 0 if the caption contains no societal critique or cynical reframing.
proposals.rationale: Applying mundane societal flaws to cartoons creates strong comedy. R20 ('second amendment') and R31 ('democratic elevator') are dense favorites, highlighting the scorecard's blind spot for sophisticated satire.

proposals.name: Internal Logic Of The Surreal
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption establishes a bizarre but internally consistent rule within the cartoon's universe that perfectly justifies the character's behavior. Score 0 if the caption jokes about the situation without establishing a coherent internal rule.
proposals.rationale: Dense rewards captions that make the absurdity make sense on its own terms. R10 (checking for faces) and R21 (freezing river) exemplify this, contrasting with dense_low items that lack this logic.

proposals.name: Rich Conversational Subtext
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the dialogue implies a complex, ongoing relationship or an action just outside the frame, rather than merely commenting on the drawing. Score 0 if the caption is a direct, superficial observation of the cartoon with no implied backstory.
proposals.rationale: Dense favors captions that expand the scene's narrative. R07 (getting rid of the lawyer) and R22 (john on the end) use rich subtext missed by the scorecard.

proposals.name: Topical Reference Integration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if a real-world cultural or topical reference is seamlessly woven into the cartoon's logic as a natural punchline. Score 0 if a topical reference is shoehorned in awkwardly without connecting to the cartoon's visual, or no reference is used.
proposals.rationale: Dense distinguishes between clever topical humor and forced jokes. R30 (six feet apart) and R59 (poop emoji) are dense favorites, while R17 (N95 mask) is a dense_low item, showing dense rewards integration over mere mention.

proposals.name: Secondary-Level Wordplay
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption features a pun or wordplay that operates on a second, less obvious level, rather than relying on a single synonym for the visual. Score 0 if the wordplay is a direct, one-to-one synonym of the visual object.
proposals.rationale: Dense heavily penalizes obvious, one-note puns that the scorecard rewards. R25 ('ewe' layered over dog/sheep ambiguity) and R43 ('elephant in the room' layered over the idiom) are dense favorites, unlike dense_low items that rely on single-level puns.

proposals.name: Dark Humor And Escalation Of Stakes
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption introduces a dark, morbid, or dangerously high-stakes implication that contrasts sharply with the innocent cartoon drawing. Score 0 if the caption maintains a light, harmless tone.
proposals.rationale: Introducing dark subtext is a hallmark of high-quality captions. R14 (eating sophomores) and R29 (cruel irony of extinction) are dense favorites missed by the scorecard.

proposals.name: Punchline Economy And Anticlimax
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption uses very few words to abruptly cut the tension or create a comedic anticlimax. Score 0 if the caption is overly wordy or explains the joke too thoroughly.
proposals.rationale: Short, punchy captions often score highly with dense models. R05 ('chicken or rabbit') and R44 ('arrive 20 minutes early') use brevity brilliantly to create an anticlimax.

proposals.name: Absurdly Specific Detail
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption uses highly specific, quirky details to sell an absurd premise, making it feel grounded in reality. Score 0 if the caption uses generic, vague statements.
proposals.rationale: Specificity enhances humor by making the absurd relatable. R27 ('three sconces and a flashlight') and R37 ('wish to end up on a deserted island with a blonde') are rewarded by the dense model.

proposals.name: Shift In Speaker Perspective
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption is spoken by an unexpected character or entity within the scene, reframing the power dynamic. Score 0 if the caption is spoken by the most obvious observer of the scene.
proposals.rationale: Dense favors captions that flip the expected perspective. R13 (dummy speaking) and R16 (report to me) shift perspective brilliantly compared to dense_low items that lack this dynamic.

proposals.name: Mundane Justification Of The Impossible
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption offers a completely practical, everyday justification for why an impossible or magical event is occurring. Score 0 if the caption merely points out the impossibility without justifying it.
proposals.rationale: Justifying the absurd is a strong comedic tool. R23 (suggested you buy a town car) and R54 (so much easier) are dense favorites because they normalize the bizarre.

proposals.name: Layered Ironic Contrast
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption presents a situation where the literal truth is deeply ironic compared to reality or the characters' oblivious expectations. Score 0 if the caption lacks ironic contrast.
proposals.rationale: Ironic twists elevate the humor. R15 (tin can to the IRS) and R40 (hoist is also a dinner table) rely on strong, layered irony favored by the dense model.

proposals.name: Topical news cycle reference
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption explicitly names or directly references a specific contemporary real-world entity, person, product, or event (e.g., 'n95 mask', 'stimulus', 'trump'). Do not judge if the reference is funny or apt, only how specific and time-bound the named entity is.
proposals.rationale: Topical references are artifacts of the submission timing and may impress a scorecard looking for cleverness, but they are not inherent qualities of the caption for that specific cartoon (e.g., R24, R28).

proposals.name: Consensus obvious idiom literalization
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption's joke relies entirely on literalizing a common idiom directly suggested by the cartoon (e.g., 'elephant in the room') or making the single most obvious pun available. Do not judge the quality of the pun, only how much it represents the consensus first-thought reading.
proposals.rationale: A scorecard might reward the neat fit of an idiom, but this often represents the consensus first-thought reading that hundreds of entrants would submit, rather than a unique angle (e.g., R35, R06).

proposals.name: Verbose conversational filler
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption uses spoken-style filler words (e.g., 'wow', 'sure', 'well', 'i guess') or conversational run-on phrasing to set up the punchline, adding words that do not change the core joke. Do not judge if the phrasing is good.
proposals.rationale: Serial entrants often know that caption contest jokes require a specific spoken rhythm, but a dense model might discount excessive verbosity that doesn't add to the visual gag (e.g., R34, R42).

proposals.name: Animal anthropomorphism justification
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption features a non-human character explicitly justifying its human-like actions by referencing its natural animal state (e.g., a bear referencing catching salmon with its mouth, a butterfly referencing nectar). Do not judge if it is funny.
proposals.rationale: This is a recognizable template for cartoon contests where the animal explains the surreal situation, which is a structural trope rather than a unique insight for the specific drawing (e.g., R20, R57).

proposals.name: Broad political or social commentary
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption invokes broader political parties, social issues, or ideological commentary (e.g., 'democratic', 'second amendment'). Do not judge the validity or humor of the commentary.
proposals.rationale: Injecting political or social commentary can impress a scorecard but is a predictable channel for engagement rather than a reflection of the cartoon's specific comedic premise (e.g., R16, R25).

proposals.name: Meta-commentary on visual absurdity
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption focuses on describing the literal absurdity of the drawing itself or pointing out the characters' mundane reaction to it (e.g., 'this is so much easier'). Do not judge if it is a good observation.
proposals.rationale: Pointing out the weirdness of the drawing or having characters flatly accept it is a standard fallback structure in caption contests that models might misread as cleverness (e.g., R21, R38).

proposals.name: Domestic or marital relationship bickering
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption frames the interaction as a mundane domestic, marital, or romantic dispute (e.g., referencing a wife, marriage, or whose turn it is to cook). Do not judge if the joke is funny or relatable.
proposals.rationale: Framing surreal scenarios as mundane relationship squabbles is a generic template that scorecards might reward for relatability, but it is not unique to the specific visual (e.g., R07, R33).

proposals.name: Extreme conversational brevity
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption is extremely short, abandoning any narrative setup to deliver a quick, blunt conversational response (e.g., 'chicken or rabbit'). Do not judge if brevity makes it a good caption.
proposals.rationale: Very short captions might be scored highly by dense models for punchiness, but they often rely on the weakest connection to the drawing, mimicking a laconic style rather than a strong premise (e.g., R12, R49).

proposals.name: Bureaucratic or corporate jargon usage
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption uses specific corporate, bureaucratic, or administrative terminology (e.g., 'downsizing', 'litigation', 'human resources'). Do not judge if it fits the drawing well.
proposals.rationale: Using corporate speak to contrast with an absurd visual is a very common contest template that mimics the magazine's historical style but is not inherently a better contest entry (e.g., R13, R02).

proposals.name: Generic-prior guessable wordplay
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption relies on a simple, highly recognizable wordplay or pun that any competent writer would immediately associate with the visual elements (e.g., 'chrysalis' for 'crisis'). Do not judge if the pun is funny.
proposals.rationale: This captures the safe, well-formed 'correct' joke that a general-purpose AI or generic writer would guess. It scores highly on generic quality but lacks the specific, surprising angle the editors actually look for (e.g., R58, R08).

proposals.name: Deadpan Absurd Normalization
proposals.instruction: Score how completely the caption treats the cartoon's bizarre, impossible situation as an ordinary, everyday occurrence. A 10 means the caption sounds like a mundane complaint, practical observation, or routine logistics applied to the surreal scene with zero acknowledgment that anything is strange. A 0 means the caption explicitly calls attention to or marvels at how weird the situation is.
proposals.rationale: The dense model strongly favors captions that deadpan the absurd. R01 ('john will pay you') treats beam-top pizza delivery as routine worksite logistics; R20 ('this is so much easier') has a bear treating grocery shopping as a minor life hack; R34 ('we will arrive 20 minutes early') reduces a magician flight attendant to a bland airline announcement. All score dense-high, card-low.

proposals.name: Implied Off-Panel World
proposals.instruction: Score how vividly the caption implies characters, events, reactions, or consequences that exist beyond the borders of the drawing. A 10 means a rich off-panel world is clearly suggested (a spouse's reaction, a neighbor's perspective, a past humiliation, a future reckoning). A 0 means everything the caption references is directly visible in the cartoon.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high entries consistently open up the world beyond the frame. R11 implies a wife's scolding ('you caught it, you clean it'); R43 imagines what downstairs neighbors must think; R48 references net-setup timing as though a larger circus event is underway. Dense-low entries like R23 ('nobody can walk out') and R08 stay entirely within what is visible.

proposals.name: Obvious-Joke Subversion
proposals.instruction: Score how well the caption avoids the single most obvious pun, wordplay, or joke available for the cartoon's premise and instead delivers a less expected angle. A 10 means the caption deliberately steers around the low-hanging fruit to find a fresher joke. A 0 means it delivers exactly the pun or joke that most people would think of first upon seeing the cartoon.
proposals.rationale: The scorecard appears to reward any detectable wordplay regardless of originality. Dense-low entries like R24 ('new phase' for a moon), R58 ('downsizing' for a miniature boss), and R31 ('mid-life chrysalis' for butterfly wings) all deliver the most predictable pun and score high card, low dense. Meanwhile dense-high R27 extends the 'elephant in the room' idiom with a twist rather than merely stating it.

proposals.name: Believable Voice Specificity
proposals.instruction: Score how naturalistically the caption reads as genuine, idiosyncratic human speech rather than a constructed joke line. A 10 means the phrasing, rhythm, and word choices sound like real dialogue you might overhear, with specific verbal tics or personality. A 0 means the caption sounds like a scripted setup-punchline with no distinct human voice.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high entries carry distinctive overheard-speech quality: R01 ('john will pay you. that's john on the end') sounds like real worksite banter; R12 ('we just need eggs, gary') has conversational exasperation; R56 ('obviously you haven't stood for hours in a freezing river…') carries weary specificity. Dense-low R45 ('so litigation continues to exist in advanced civilizations') reads as an intellectual construction, not speech.

proposals.name: Unexpected Speaker Assignment
proposals.instruction: Score how surprising yet apt the choice of speaker or perspective is relative to what the drawing most obviously suggests. A 10 means the caption gives voice to a character or viewpoint that is unexpected but makes perfect sense, recontextualizing the entire scene. A 0 means the speaker is exactly who the viewer would assume is talking.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high captions often shift the expected speaker. R02 gives voice to the miniature boss figure as 'the coward behind me'; R05 has the mocked HR dummy confront its tormenter; R56 gives the bear a weary justification for grocery shopping. These unexpected-voice choices create depth the scorecard does not capture.

proposals.name: Cross-Domain Conceptual Bridge
proposals.instruction: Score how effectively the caption connects the cartoon's visual situation to an entirely unrelated conceptual domain (law, politics, economics, romance, bureaucracy) in a way that generates fresh meaning. A 10 means the foreign domain illuminates the cartoon in a surprising and coherent new way. A 0 means the caption stays entirely within the cartoon's own obvious conceptual world.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high entries frequently bridge domains: R28 connects aliens to the Second Amendment; R33 reframes engine-compartment clowns as a legal billing problem; R36 turns the elephant-elevator scene into political commentary. Dense-low R18 ('special tonight—spare ribs') stays safely inside the food-domain pun the visual already suggests.

proposals.name: Compound Layering on Reread
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption contains multiple layers of humor or meaning that compound upon reflection, rewarding a second or third reading. A 10 means each rereading reveals an additional joke, implication, or structural connection that makes the caption funnier. A 0 means the entire joke is fully delivered on first contact with nothing left to discover.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high entries reward rereading: R27's elephant idiom extension gains layers once you parse the room-vs-elevator distinction; R29's 'town car' works simultaneously as a Lincoln model and as a car full of town clowns; R54's wish-fulfillment irony deepens with each clause. Dense-low single-pun entries like R24 and R58 deliver everything on first read.

proposals.name: Social Power-Dynamic Insight
proposals.instruction: Score how interestingly the caption reveals, creates, or complicates a hierarchy, power struggle, or social relationship between depicted characters. A 10 means the caption exposes a specific, nuanced social dynamic that transforms how you read the drawing. A 0 means no social dynamic is present or the dynamic is entirely obvious.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high office cartoons generate complex power dynamics: R02 ('the coward behind me. that's who's firing you') creates a three-way power struggle; R05 gives the mocked dummy a position of vengeful authority; R16 ('ignore him. you now report directly to me') stages a chain-of-command coup. Dense-low R58 ('downsizing') merely notes the smallness without any social depth.

proposals.name: Multi-Element Visual Integration
proposals.instruction: Score how many distinct visual elements from the drawing the caption ties together into a single coherent joke or observation. A 10 means three or more specific visual details are each essential to the humor and they interlock. A 0 means the caption engages with only one visual element or could work for many different cartoons equally well.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high entries weave multiple elements together: R25 ties the catcher's mask, six-foot spacing, and the living-room baseball game into one COVID-era observation; R43 connects bowling balls, the rolling pin, and imagined downstairs neighbors; R48 links the cannon, the party context, and a practical question about nets. Dense-low R24 engages with only the moon.

proposals.name: Topical Reference Self-Sufficiency
proposals.instruction: Score how well the caption's humor stands on its own without relying on a topical, cultural, or celebrity reference as the primary comedic engine. A 10 means the caption is fully self-sufficient—any reference present is incidental to a joke that works on its own terms, or no reference is needed at all. A 0 means the caption's entire comedic value depends on recognizing a specific topical reference and removing it leaves nothing.
proposals.rationale: The scorecard appears to reward topical references regardless of integration. Dense-low R41 ('easier to get than an N95 mask') and R53 ('his full 1200 stimulus') use the reference as the entire joke. Dense-high R25 embeds COVID references (masks, six feet) as secondary details inside a richer baseball scenario, and R40's ten-dollar-beer complaint is organic to the domestic situation.

proposals.name: Comedic Efficiency
proposals.instruction: Score how much comedic impact the caption achieves relative to its length, with no wasted words. A 10 means every word is load-bearing—the caption is maximally funny for its brevity and nothing could be cut. A 0 means the caption is padded, over-explained, or has low joke-to-word density.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high entries are strikingly efficient: R01 packs characterization, humor, and scene-resolution into nine words; R34 ('and we will arrive 20 minutes early') is a perfect five-word tonal gag; R20 ('this is so much easier. i wish i thought of it sooner') does enormous work in ten words. Dense-low R45 is wordy and intellectual but yields little humor per word.

proposals.name: Petty-Stakes Emotional Grounding
proposals.instruction: Score how specifically and relatably a depicted character is invested in a small, human-scale concern—petty grievance, minor inconvenience, domestic anxiety, social embarrassment—rather than the grand absurdity of the scene. A 10 means the character's emotional investment is vivid, relatable, and comically disproportionate to the surreal situation. A 0 means no specific emotional investment is conveyed.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high entries ground surreal scenes in petty emotions: R40's outrage over ten-dollar beer charges amid a living-room baseball game; R54's recursive disappointment about a wish gone wrong; R56's bear complaining about the hardship of river-fishing with your mouth. These granular emotional stakes separate great entries from merely clever ones.

proposals.name: Setup-to-Payoff Register Shift
proposals.instruction: Score how effectively the caption's opening words set up one expectation—emotional, tonal, or topical—and then deliver the payoff in a deliberately different register. A 10 means the gap between setup and payoff registers is wide and surprising yet perfectly coherent. A 0 means the setup leads predictably and linearly to its conclusion with no tonal pivot.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high entries frequently pivot between registers mid-caption: R25 opens as COVID commentary but lands as casual baseball banter; R42 opens as a dramatic rescue line but reveals it is about dinner; R54 opens with mutual disappointment but pivots to a wish-gone-wrong backstory. Dense-low R24 ('well this is a new phase') never shifts register at all.

proposals.name: Self-Aware Absurdity Within Frame
proposals.instruction: Score how well the caption demonstrates awareness of its own absurdity—commenting on or exploiting the surreal situation's internal logic—while remaining fully in-character and never breaking the fictional frame. A 10 means the caption winks at the absurdity through the character's own voice and logic, deepening the joke. A 0 means either no awareness of the absurdity whatsoever or an explicit fourth-wall-breaking commentary.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high entries stay in-frame while being meta: R14 ('cruel irony if we go extinct but those hats endure') comments on absurdity through dinosaur logic; R26 ('personally i prefer the taste of sophomores') uses the propeller hat to darkly subvert college-humor expectations; R46 ('your hat says, i have chosen not to mate') reads an absurd visual detail as a devastating social signal.

proposals.name: Specificity to Unique Visual Detail
proposals.instruction: Score how tightly the caption's humor depends on the specific, unique details of this particular cartoon rather than on a generic category it belongs to. A 10 means the caption could ONLY work for this exact drawing—its humor is inseparable from the specific visual premise. A 0 means the caption could work equally well for many different cartoons sharing the same general subject.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high captions exploit visual specificity: R07's 'ewe/you' pun only works because sheep and dogs look nearly identical in this drawing; R60's 'check for faces—I once barked at a cotton bale' is inseparable from the fluffy-confusion premise. Dense-low R24 ('new phase') could accompany any moon cartoon, and R31 ('mid-life chrysalis') could work for any butterfly-man image interchangeably.

proposals.name: Topical news cycle references
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption incorporates specific, real-world contemporary news events, political figures, or temporary social trends (e.g., pandemics, specific politicians, economic stimuli). Do not judge if the reference is funny or appropriate.
proposals.rationale: A model might score these highly for cleverness without recognizing they are highly perishable. R35 ('n95 mask') and R57 ('trump cancelled the crusades') lean heavily on very specific temporal contexts, unlike evergreen absurdist entries like R38.

proposals.name: Generic-prior obvious idiom
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption relies on the single most obvious idiom, pun, or literal interpretation directly invited by the visual elements of the scene. Do not judge whether the joke is clever or well-executed.
proposals.rationale: General models often over-reward the consensus 'first-thought' reading of an image because it perfectly aligns text and image. R10 ('elephant in the room') and R23 ('downsizing') are the most predictable puns for their respective cartoons.

proposals.name: All-lowercase transcription style
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the text lacks standard capitalization entirely, utilizing all lowercase letters for what would normally be proper nouns or the start of sentences. Do not judge the readability or grammatical correctness.
proposals.rationale: The visible text shows many entries are transcribed completely in lowercase (R01, R13, R54). This formatting quirk can bias a model that latches onto specific typographical styles rather than semantic content.

proposals.name: Practised entrant dialogue brevity
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption is composed of short, punchy spoken dialogue without any narrative setup, character description, or internal monologue tags. Do not judge if the dialogue is effective or humorous.
proposals.rationale: Serial contest entrants often adopt a highly disciplined, minimalist dialogue style that strips away all scene-setting. R04 ('chicken or rabbit') and R59 ('and we will arrive 20 minutes early') exhibit this terse, practised rhythm, which is textually recognizable but not inherently the same as being the best joke.

proposals.name: Conversational filler and throat-clearing
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption includes conversational filler phrases, rhetorical framing devices, or throat-clearing before delivering the main point (e.g., 'remind me again,' 'the worst part is'). Do not judge whether this framing helps the joke.
proposals.rationale: Captions like R05 ('remind me again...') and R07 ('the worst part is...') use naturalistic padding to force a conversational tone. A dense model may perceive this as authentic voice, but it is often just a stylistic crutch.

proposals.name: Politically divisive angle
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption introduces a politically divisive, legally controversial, or culturally polarized real-world subject that is entirely absent from the drawing itself. Do not judge the appropriateness or humor of the subject.
proposals.rationale: Jokes that inject partisan or edgy real-world politics into an apolitical drawing can trigger engagement spikes that models mistake for universal quality. R08 ('democratic elevator') and R15 ('second amendment') rely heavily on this divisive textural fingerprint.

proposals.name: Adjacent cultural trope reliance
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption maps the visual scene onto a highly standardized pop-culture or occupational trope (e.g., musicians arguing about the band, real estate agent tropes). Do not judge if the mapping is amusing.
proposals.rationale: When a drawing features a specific setting (like dinosaurs with instruments), there is a predictable flood of entries using standard tropes. R46 ('stairway to heaven') and R55 ('we're not cancelling rehearsal') rely on standard musical tropes rather than unique observations of the drawing.

proposals.name: Digital era slang and entities
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption uses vocabulary, slang, or specific entities native to 2010s-2020s digital culture (e.g., emojis, apps, modern tech billionaires). Do not judge the relevance of the term.
proposals.rationale: Captions referencing modern digital life, such as R33 ('poop emoji') and R06 ('elon musk'), are instantly dateable to a specific cultural era. A model might score these highly for perceived cleverness without discounting their narrow temporal window.

proposals.name: Safe metaphorical reframing
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption completely ignores the physical absurdity of the drawing in favor of treating the scene as a polite metaphor for everyday life (e.g., relationships, personal growth). Do not judge the wisdom of the metaphor.
proposals.rationale: R49 ('yes, you are good for them...') and R42 ('i can't keep waiting for you to evolve') treat surreal images as tame relationship metaphors. A scorecard model may reward this safe, recognizable structure as good writing, even if it misses the contest's typical absurdity.

proposals.name: Homophone and literal wordplay density
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption heavily features simple homophones, double-meanings, or direct literalizations that explicitly rely on the concrete objects in the drawing (e.g., animal sounds, food puns). Do not judge if the pun is funny.
proposals.rationale: R24 ('ewe, ewe') and R51 ('spare ribs') utilize basic wordplay that is heavily over-represented in amateur caption contests. Models often flag these as high-signal semantic matches despite the wordplay being a generic surface-level construction rather than an inventive joke.
